Exactly seven calendar days' advance notice transmitted via digital social media channels and published in an English daily newspaper in Mumbai.
A minimum of twenty-one (21) clear days' notice in writing must be given to all members entitled to attend and vote at the Annual General Meeting.
explanationCorrect: Under Council Guidelines for Conducting AGM (approved 2 March 2013), a minimum of 21 clear days' notice in writing is mandatory for convening an AGM.
explanationIncorrect: The statutory and guideline standard for an AGM is 21 clear days' notice in writing to all voting members.

source: IAI Governance, Council Guidelines (Principles & Procedures for GNs/APSs)
question: Under the Council Guidelines for issuance of Guidance Notes (GNs) and Actuarial Practice Standards (APSs) Versions 3, 4, and 5, what is the standard public consultation window for an Exposure Draft?
options: The Exposure Draft must be published on the IAI website for public consultation and member feedback for a period of thirty (30) to sixty (60) days.
The Exposure Draft must remain open for public comment for a mandatory minimum of twelve months across three consecutive financial years.
Zero public consultation is required; the President can enact an APS immediately as a binding standard upon signing the draft in Council.
The Exposure Draft is circulated confidentially to elected Council members only for forty-eight hours without any public or general member consultation.
explanationCorrect: Under standard setting due process (Versions 3, 4, 5), new APS/GN exposure drafts are published for 30 to 60 days for public and member feedback.
explanationIncorrect: Standard setting due process mandates a 30 to 60 day exposure draft period on the website to ensure broad public and professional consultation.

source: IAI Governance, Council Guidelines (Social Media Usage & Reputation - Feb 2026)
question: Under the Council Guidelines on 'Use of Social Media and Reputation of the Profession' (dated February 2026), what is the core standard governing members' online conduct?
options: Members may freely publish unverified confidential client valuation results on digital forums provided the post is deleted within twenty-four hours.
Members must uphold professional dignity online and are strictly liable for posts that disparage the Institute, breach confidentiality, or harm professional reputation.
Members are completely immune from disciplinary action for personal social media posts, provided they state 'views expressed are purely personal'.
Members are prohibited from maintaining personal profiles on LinkedIn, Twitter, or professional networking platforms under threat of expulsion.
explanationCorrect: The February 2026 Social Media Guidelines hold members professionally accountable for digital commentary, prohibiting disparagement, confidentiality breaches, and disrepute.
explanationIncorrect: Disclaimers like 'views are personal' do not shield members from disciplinary accountability for unprofessional or defamatory social media conduct.

source: IAI Governance, Council Guidelines (Advisory on New Labor Codes - 27 Jan 2026)
question: Under the IAI Advisory on the implementation of New Labor Codes for employee benefit valuation (dated 27 January 2026), what guidance is provided to actuaries valuing gratuity liabilities?
options: Actuaries must ignore the New Labor Codes entirely until all state government judicial challenges are definitively settled by the Supreme Court.
Actuaries are forbidden from certifying any employee benefit valuation report until the Ministry of Labour issues company-specific actuarial guidelines.
Actuaries must assess the redefined definition of 'wages' (50% cap on allowances) and evaluate its material financial impact on gratuity and leave encashment reserves.
Actuaries must immediately write off all existing corporate gratuity liabilities and replace them with defined contribution provident fund accounting entries.
explanationCorrect: The 27 Jan 2026 Advisory directs actuaries to evaluate the impact of the amended 'wages' definition (50% allowances rule) on gratuity and employee benefit liabilities.
explanationIncorrect: Actuaries cannot ignore enacted legislation; they must actively model and disclose the impact of the new wage structure on statutory liabilities.

source: IAI Governance & Actuaries Act 2006, Section 43 (Quality Review Board)
question: Under Section 43 of the Actuaries Act, 2006 and official IAI governance records, who constitutes the Quality Review Board (QRB) and who serves as its Chairperson?
options: The QRB is constituted by the Council of the Institute, headed by the President of the Institute ex-officio alongside six senior Appointed Actuaries.
The QRB is established by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority, headed by the Member (Actuarial) alongside state high court judges.
The QRB is an informal standing subcommittee of the Professionalism Committee, headed by the Honorary Secretary of the Institute on an annual rotational basis.
The QRB is constituted by the Central Government, headed by Chairperson Supratim Bandyopadhyay, alongside four part-time members serving a three-year term.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 43(1), the Central Government constitutes the Quality Review Board, consisting of a Chairperson (Supratim Bandyopadhyay) and 4 members (3-year tenure).
explanationIncorrect: The QRB is appointed by the Central Government under Section 43, not by Council, IRDAI, or the Professionalism Committee.

source: IAI Governance, Quality Review Board - Sec 43 (Composition Breakdown)
question: Under the official governance notifications on the IAI website regarding the Quality Review Board under Section 43, how are the four members of the Board nominated?
options: Two members are nominated by the Central Government and two members are nominated by the Council of the Institute, serving three-year part-time appointments.
Three members are nominated by life insurance companies and one member is nominated by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
All four members are nominated directly by the President of the Institute from among Fellows with twenty years of continuous actuarial practice experience.
Four members are elected directly by registered student and Associate members through a nationwide electronic voting ballot conducted every two years.
explanationCorrect: The QRB consists of a Chairperson plus 4 members: 2 nominated by Central Government (Sanjeev Kumar Pujari, G. Ramaswamy) and 2 nominated by Council (Gopal Kumar Vishwanath Roy, Padmaja Raghunathan).
explanationIncorrect: The QRB composition is strictly split: 2 nominated by Central Government and 2 nominated by Council, serving part-time 3-year tenures.

source: IAI Governance & Actuaries Act 2006, Section 44 (Functions of QRB)
question: Under Section 44 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, which of the following accurately describes the three statutory functions of the Quality Review Board?
options: To conduct disciplinary trials against accused members, impose monetary fines up to Rs. 10 Lakhs, and issue formal reprimands under statutory procedures.
To fix standards for services provided by members, review quality of services including actuarial audit, and guide members on improving service quality.
To manage the annual investments of the Institute's pension funds, negotiate corporate employee salaries, and set registration fees for student examinations.
To register new insurance companies with the IRDAI, approve life insurance product brochures, and license commercial reinsurance brokers in India.
explanationCorrect: Section 44 mandates three functions: (a) fix standards for services, (b) review quality of services including actuarial audit, and (c) guide members on quality and statutory compliance.
explanationIncorrect: The QRB is a quality advisory and review body; it does not conduct disciplinary trials, manage staff salaries, or license insurance companies.

question: Under official IAI website governance records, which statutory rules govern the procedure for meetings, terms of service, and allowances of the Chairperson and Members of the Quality Review Board?
options: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority (Appointed Actuary) Regulations 2022 governing corporate governance in public limited insurers.
The Civil Procedure Code 1908 governing administrative hearings and commercial arbitrations before the High Court of Judicature at Bombay.
The Actuaries Quality Review Board (Procedure for Meetings, and Terms and Conditions of Service and Allowances of Chairperson and Members) Rules, 2008.
The Institute of Actuaries of India General Internal Operating By-Laws and Standing Orders enacted by the Executive Director in 2012.
explanationCorrect: The QRB meetings, allowances, and service conditions are governed by the Actuaries Quality Review Board Rules, 2008 enacted by the Central Government.
explanationIncorrect: The specific governing rules are the Actuaries Quality Review Board Rules, 2008, not the CPC 1908 or IRDAI Appointed Actuary Regulations.

question: According to the official Council directory on the IAI website, who are the current executive Office Bearers leading the Institute of Actuaries of India?
options: President Supratim Bandyopadhyay, Vice President Sanjeev Kumar Pujari, and Honorary Secretary G. Ramaswamy, appointed directly by the Ministry of Finance.
A rotating triumvirate of Chief Executive Officers representing the largest three general insurance companies in India serving ex-officio.
President Kartikey Kandoi, Vice President K S Gopalakrishnan, and Honorary Secretary Pravir Chandra, appointed for five-year non-renewable terms.
President K S Gopalakrishnan, Vice President Pravir Chandra, and Honorary Secretary Kartikey Kandoi, serving one-year elected terms from among Council members.
explanationCorrect: The current IAI Office Bearers are President K S Gopalakrishnan, Vice President Pravir Chandra, and Honorary Secretary Kartikey Kandoi.
explanationIncorrect: Supratim Bandyopadhyay is Chairperson of QRB. Office Bearers are elected annually by Council from amongst elected members.

source: IAI Governance, Council Nominees under Section 12(1)(b)
question: Under Section 12(1)(b) of the Act and official notifications on the IAI website, who are the Central Government nominees currently serving on the Council?
options: Shri Debasish Prusty (Notification 11/06/2026), Ms. Girija Subramanian (19/08/2025), and Shri R. Doraiswamy (19/08/2025), representing the Government of India.
Three executive directors of commercial public sector banks appointed on an honorary basis to manage the Institute's cash and treasury reserves.
Four sitting judges of the Supreme Court of India nominated directly by the Chief Justice to supervise professional ethics investigations.
Two joint secretaries from the Ministry of Corporate Affairs and two regional directors from the Reserve Bank of India serving five-year tenures.
explanationCorrect: Government of India nominees on the IAI Council include Shri Debasish Prusty, Ms. Girija Subramanian, and Shri R. Doraiswamy pursuant to official Gazette notifications.
explanationIncorrect: The Central Government nominees represent public financial governance, not the judiciary, commercial bank treasury departments, or the RBI.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 28 & Disciplinary Rules 2008, Rule 9
question: Under Section 28 of the Actuaries Act, 2006 and Rule 9 of the Disciplinary Rules 2008, what is the role of the Director (Discipline) and within what timeframe must a prima facie opinion be formed?
options: Serves as legal defense counsel for accused members before the Appellate Authority and cross-examines complainants during high court appeals.
Acts as the investigative gatekeeper, receives complaints/information, conducts preliminary examination, and issues a prima facie opinion within 60 days.
Conducts judicial trials, delivers final sentencing verdicts against respondents, and collects monetary disciplinary fines within 14 calendar days.
Audits the commercial books of the Institute and decides whether to approve annual membership certificate renewals for practicing consultants.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 28 and Rule 9, the Director (Discipline) investigates complaints/information and submits a prima facie opinion to the Board or Committee within 60 days.
explanationIncorrect: The Director (Discipline) is an investigative officer who forms a prima facie opinion; final adjudication is conducted by the Board of Discipline or Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 29 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what is the jurisdiction of the Board of Discipline and what maximum penalties can it impose?
options: Deals with fee disputes between consulting actuaries and can order commercial compensation payments up to Rs. 25 Lakhs to the client.
Deals with criminal fraud charges and can order custodial imprisonment for up to two years in a central correctional penitentiary.
Deals exclusively with First Schedule misconduct; can reprimand the member, suspend membership up to three months, or impose a fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh.
Deals exclusively with Second Schedule misconduct; can permanently expel the member from the Institute or impose a fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 29, the Board of Discipline handles First Schedule matters and can reprimand, suspend membership up to 3 months, or fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh.
explanationIncorrect: First Schedule matters fall under the Board of Discipline (cap Rs. 1 Lakh, suspension up to 3 months). Second Schedule falls under the Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 29B of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what is the jurisdiction of the Disciplinary Committee and what maximum penalties can it impose?
options: Deals with internal staff grievances within the Secretariat and can adjust employee salaries or reassign departmental office workstations.
Deals exclusively with routine administrative fee defaults; can issue informal advisory warnings with zero authority to suspend practice licenses.
Deals exclusively with overseas actuarial bodies and can negotiate reciprocal exemption treaties with foreign professional councils.
Deals with Second Schedule or combined First and Second Schedule misconduct; can reprimand, remove permanently, or fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 29B, the Disciplinary Committee handles Second Schedule or combined cases and can reprimand, remove permanently/temporarily, or fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanationIncorrect: The Disciplinary Committee handles grave misconduct under the Second Schedule, with powers to permanently expel members and fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.

question: Under Rules 4 and 5 of the Actuaries (Procedure for Enquiry of Professional and Other Misconduct) Rules, 2008, what are the statutory timelines for submitting the Written Statement and Rejoinder?
options: The respondent has 21 days from receipt of complaint to submit a Written Statement; the complainant has 21 days from receipt of the statement to submit a Rejoinder.
The respondent has 10 calendar days to respond verbally; the complainant has 48 hours to file a formal cross-examination questionnaire before Council.
There are zero statutory timelines; parties may submit pleadings at their leisure until the Council President formally schedules an oral hearing session.
The respondent has 60 days to file a defense statement; the complainant has 90 days to lodge an interlocutory rejoinder petition before the Council.
explanationCorrect: The Disciplinary Rules 2008 establish a symmetrical 21-day timeline: 21 days for the respondent's Written Statement, and 21 days for the complainant's Rejoinder.
explanationIncorrect: Pleadings follow strict statutory windows: exactly 21 days for Written Statement and 21 days for Rejoinder under Rules 4 and 5.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 31 (Powers of Civil Court)
question: Under Section 31 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what legal powers are vested in the Disciplinary Directorate, the Board of Discipline, and the Disciplinary Committee?
options: Vested with zero legal discovery powers; they can only review documents voluntarily provided by the complainant and accused member.
Vested with the same powers as a Civil Court under CPC 1908: summoning witnesses, discovery/production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits.
Vested with summary arbitral powers to modify commercial consulting fees and renegotiate contractual indemnities between corporate disputants.
Vested with full jurisdiction of a Criminal Sessions Court under the CrPC to conduct criminal trials and execute custodial sentences.
explanationCorrect: Section 31 vests the disciplinary authorities with powers of a Civil Court under the CPC 1908: summoning persons, inspecting documents, and taking evidence on oath.
explanationIncorrect: Disciplinary tribunals exercise Civil Court powers under Section 31, not criminal sentencing powers or commercial contract renegotiation authority.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 6 (Prohibition on Soliciting Clients)
question: Actuary Rajesh Sharma, in public practice, sends unsolicited circular emails to Chief Financial Officers of all listed companies offering discounted pension valuation fees. Under the First Schedule, how is this conduct classified?
options: Permissible conduct provided the solicitation emails are reviewed and approved in advance by the Institute's External Affairs Committee.
Legitimate commercial outreach; modern digital marketing principles permit direct email solicitation provided the technical fee schedule is disclosed.
Professional misconduct in practice; an actuary in practice cannot solicit clients or professional work directly or indirectly by circulars, advertisements, or personal canvassing.
A minor procedural irregularity that can be excused provided the actuary secures at least two corporate client appointments from the campaign.
explanationCorrect: Clause 6 of Part I of the First Schedule explicitly classifies soliciting clients or professional work by circular, advertisement, or canvassing as professional misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Direct commercial solicitation of clients violates First Schedule Part I Clause 6, compromising professional dignity and public trust.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 8 (Duty to Communicate with Predecessor)
question: Actuary Priya Venkat accepts an appointment as Appointed Actuary of an insurance company without first communicating in writing with the retiring actuary. Under the First Schedule, how is this characterized?
options: Misconduct only if the outgoing actuary had been dismissed by the corporate board of directors for reasons involving documented fraud.
Acceptable professional practice provided the new actuary completes the statutory valuation on time and files the required regulatory solvency forms.
A commercial matter between the two actuaries that does not fall within the statutory disciplinary jurisdiction of the Institute of Actuaries of India.
Professional misconduct; accepting a position as an actuary previously held by another actuary without first communicating with them in writing constitutes statutory misconduct.
explanationCorrect: Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule makes it professional misconduct to accept an appointment without first communicating in writing with the incumbent actuary.
explanationIncorrect: Written communication with the predecessor is a mandatory statutory duty under First Schedule Part I Clause 8; failure to do so constitutes misconduct.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 7 (Gross Negligence)
question: Actuary Vikramaditya Rao signs a statutory valuation report certifying insurer solvency without reviewing policy data or testing claims triangles, resulting in massive insolvency. Under which Schedule does this gross negligence fall?
options: Second Schedule Part I (Clause 7); gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties is a severe offence adjudicated by the Disciplinary Committee.
Exempt from disciplinary proceedings under the Actuaries Act provided the insurer's external auditors also signed off on the statutory accounts.
First Schedule Part II; gross negligence applies exclusively to salaried employees in commercial retail banks rather than consulting actuaries.
First Schedule Part I; routine mathematical calculation errors are minor professional infractions handled informally by the Board of Discipline.
explanationCorrect: Gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties constitutes severe misconduct under Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule, subject to permanent removal.
explanationIncorrect: Gross negligence falls under the Second Schedule (not First Schedule), carrying serious penalties up to permanent expulsion and Rs. 5 Lakhs fine.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 5 & 6 (Concealing Material Misstatement)
question: An actuary knows that a client's financial statements contain a catastrophic 40% understatement of unearned premium reserves, but certifies the balance sheet without qualification. Under the Second Schedule, what is the consequence?
options: Immune from liability under Institute regulations because an actuary owes an absolute commercial fiduciary duty to protect client financial solvency.
Guilty of professional misconduct under Second Schedule Part I for failing to report a material misstatement known to them or gross negligence.
Subject to a mandatory maximum fine of Rs. 1,000 imposed by a local judicial magistrate with zero professional disciplinary consequences.
Guilty only of a minor clerical omission that can be resolved by filing an amended addendum with the insurance company board within six months.
explanationCorrect: Under Second Schedule Part I (Clauses 5 & 6), failing to disclose a material fact known to them or failing to report a material misstatement constitutes grave misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Concealing material reserve understatements constitutes severe Second Schedule misconduct, exposing the member to permanent expulsion by the Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 36 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, where can a member aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or Disciplinary Committee file an appeal, and within what timeframe?
options: To the Quality Review Board sitting as an administrative court of appeal, filed within fourteen calendar days of the penalty announcement.
To the President of the Institute of Actuaries of India sitting in executive chambers, filed within thirty calendar days of the decision.
To the Appellate Authority established under Section 36 of the Act, filed within ninety (90) days from the date of communication of the order.
To the local municipal district civil court in Mumbai, filed within twelve months accompanied by an appeal deposit of Rs. 10 Lakhs.
explanationCorrect: Section 36 provides that any member aggrieved by an order of the Board or Committee may appeal to the Appellate Authority within 90 days of communication.
explanationIncorrect: Appeals lie to the Appellate Authority under Section 36 within 90 days, not to the QRB, the Institute President, or a municipal district court.

question: Actuary Vikramaditya Rao, in public practice, sends unsolicited circular emails to Chief Financial Officers of all listed companies offering discounted pension valuation fees. Under the First Schedule, how is this conduct classified?

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 8 (Duty to Communicate with Predecessor)
question: Actuary Ananya Sengupta accepts an appointment as Appointed Actuary of an insurance company without first communicating in writing with the retiring actuary. Under the First Schedule, how is this characterized?

question: An actuary knows that a client's financial statements contain a catastrophic 40% understatement of unearned premium reserves, but certifies the balance sheet without qualification. Under the Second Schedule, what is the consequence?

explanationIncorrect: Concealing material reserve understatements constitutes severe Second Schedule misconduct, exposing the member to permanent expulsion by the Disciplinary Committee.

options: Misconduct only if the outgoing actuary had been dismissed by the corporate board of directors for reasons involving documented fraud.
Professional misconduct; accepting a position as an actuary previously held by another actuary without first communicating with them in writing constitutes statutory misconduct.
A commercial matter between the two actuaries that does not fall within the statutory disciplinary jurisdiction of the Institute of Actuaries of India.
Acceptable professional practice provided the new actuary completes the statutory valuation on time and files the required regulatory solvency forms.
explanationCorrect: Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule makes it professional misconduct to accept an appointment without first communicating in writing with the incumbent actuary.
explanationIncorrect: Written communication with the predecessor is a mandatory statutory duty under First Schedule Part I Clause 8; failure to do so constitutes misconduct.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 7 (Gross Negligence)
question: Actuary Sunita Deshmukh signs a statutory valuation report certifying insurer solvency without reviewing policy data or testing claims triangles, resulting in massive insolvency. Under which Schedule does this gross negligence fall?
options: First Schedule Part II; gross negligence applies exclusively to salaried employees in commercial retail banks rather than consulting actuaries.
Exempt from disciplinary proceedings under the Actuaries Act provided the insurer's external auditors also signed off on the statutory accounts.
Second Schedule Part I (Clause 7); gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties is a severe offence adjudicated by the Disciplinary Committee.
First Schedule Part I; routine mathematical calculation errors are minor professional infractions handled informally by the Board of Discipline.
explanationCorrect: Gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties constitutes severe misconduct under Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule, subject to permanent removal.
explanationIncorrect: Gross negligence falls under the Second Schedule (not First Schedule), carrying serious penalties up to permanent expulsion and Rs. 5 Lakhs fine.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 5 & 6 (Concealing Material Misstatement)
question: An actuary knows that a client's financial statements contain a catastrophic 40% understatement of unearned premium reserves, but certifies the balance sheet without qualification. Under the Second Schedule, what is the consequence?
options: Guilty only of a minor clerical omission that can be resolved by filing an amended addendum with the insurance company board within six months.
Immune from liability under Institute regulations because an actuary owes an absolute commercial fiduciary duty to protect client financial solvency.
Subject to a mandatory maximum fine of Rs. 1,000 imposed by a local judicial magistrate with zero professional disciplinary consequences.
Guilty of professional misconduct under Second Schedule Part I for failing to report a material misstatement known to them or gross negligence.
explanationCorrect: Under Second Schedule Part I (Clauses 5 & 6), failing to disclose a material fact known to them or failing to report a material misstatement constitutes grave misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Concealing material reserve understatements constitutes severe Second Schedule misconduct, exposing the member to permanent expulsion by the Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 36 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, where can a member aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or Disciplinary Committee file an appeal, and within what timeframe?
options: To the Appellate Authority established under Section 36 of the Act, filed within ninety (90) days from the date of communication of the order.
To the Quality Review Board sitting as an administrative court of appeal, filed within fourteen calendar days of the penalty announcement.
To the local municipal district civil court in Mumbai, filed within twelve months accompanied by an appeal deposit of Rs. 10 Lakhs.
To the President of the Institute of Actuaries of India sitting in executive chambers, filed within thirty calendar days of the decision.
explanationCorrect: Section 36 provides that any member aggrieved by an order of the Board or Committee may appeal to the Appellate Authority within 90 days of communication.
explanationIncorrect: Appeals lie to the Appellate Authority under Section 36 within 90 days, not to the QRB, the Institute President, or a municipal district court.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 28 & Disciplinary Rules 2008, Rule 9
question: Under Section 28 of the Actuaries Act, 2006 and Rule 9 of the Disciplinary Rules 2008, what is the role of the Director (Discipline) and within what timeframe must a prima facie opinion be formed?
options: Audits the commercial books of the Institute and decides whether to approve annual membership certificate renewals for practicing consultants.
Acts as the investigative gatekeeper, receives complaints/information, conducts preliminary examination, and issues a prima facie opinion within 60 days.
Serves as legal defense counsel for accused members before the Appellate Authority and cross-examines complainants during high court appeals.
Conducts judicial trials, delivers final sentencing verdicts against respondents, and collects monetary disciplinary fines within 14 calendar days.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 28 and Rule 9, the Director (Discipline) investigates complaints/information and submits a prima facie opinion to the Board or Committee within 60 days.
explanationIncorrect: The Director (Discipline) is an investigative officer who forms a prima facie opinion; final adjudication is conducted by the Board of Discipline or Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 29 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what is the jurisdiction of the Board of Discipline and what maximum penalties can it impose?
options: Deals with criminal fraud charges and can order custodial imprisonment for up to two years in a central correctional penitentiary.
Deals exclusively with Second Schedule misconduct; can permanently expel the member from the Institute or impose a fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
Deals exclusively with First Schedule misconduct; can reprimand the member, suspend membership up to three months, or impose a fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh.
Deals with fee disputes between consulting actuaries and can order commercial compensation payments up to Rs. 25 Lakhs to the client.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 29, the Board of Discipline handles First Schedule matters and can reprimand, suspend membership up to 3 months, or fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh.
explanationIncorrect: First Schedule matters fall under the Board of Discipline (cap Rs. 1 Lakh, suspension up to 3 months). Second Schedule falls under the Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 29B of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what is the jurisdiction of the Disciplinary Committee and what maximum penalties can it impose?
options: Deals exclusively with routine administrative fee defaults; can issue informal advisory warnings with zero authority to suspend practice licenses.
Deals exclusively with overseas actuarial bodies and can negotiate reciprocal exemption treaties with foreign professional councils.
Deals with internal staff grievances within the Secretariat and can adjust employee salaries or reassign departmental office workstations.
Deals with Second Schedule or combined First and Second Schedule misconduct; can reprimand, remove permanently, or fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 29B, the Disciplinary Committee handles Second Schedule or combined cases and can reprimand, remove permanently/temporarily, or fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanationIncorrect: The Disciplinary Committee handles grave misconduct under the Second Schedule, with powers to permanently expel members and fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.

question: Under Rules 4 and 5 of the Actuaries (Procedure for Enquiry of Professional and Other Misconduct) Rules, 2008, what are the statutory timelines for submitting the Written Statement and Rejoinder?
options: The respondent has 21 days from receipt of complaint to submit a Written Statement; the complainant has 21 days from receipt of the statement to submit a Rejoinder.
There are zero statutory timelines; parties may submit pleadings at their leisure until the Council President formally schedules an oral hearing session.
The respondent has 10 calendar days to respond verbally; the complainant has 48 hours to file a formal cross-examination questionnaire before Council.
The respondent has 60 days to file a defense statement; the complainant has 90 days to lodge an interlocutory rejoinder petition before the Council.
explanationCorrect: The Disciplinary Rules 2008 establish a symmetrical 21-day timeline: 21 days for the respondent's Written Statement, and 21 days for the complainant's Rejoinder.
explanationIncorrect: Pleadings follow strict statutory windows: exactly 21 days for Written Statement and 21 days for Rejoinder under Rules 4 and 5.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 31 (Powers of Civil Court)
question: Under Section 31 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what legal powers are vested in the Disciplinary Directorate, the Board of Discipline, and the Disciplinary Committee?
options: Vested with full jurisdiction of a Criminal Sessions Court under the CrPC to conduct criminal trials and execute custodial sentences.
Vested with the same powers as a Civil Court under CPC 1908: summoning witnesses, discovery/production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits.
Vested with zero legal discovery powers; they can only review documents voluntarily provided by the complainant and accused member.
Vested with summary arbitral powers to modify commercial consulting fees and renegotiate contractual indemnities between corporate disputants.
explanationCorrect: Section 31 vests the disciplinary authorities with powers of a Civil Court under the CPC 1908: summoning persons, inspecting documents, and taking evidence on oath.
explanationIncorrect: Disciplinary tribunals exercise Civil Court powers under Section 31, not criminal sentencing powers or commercial contract renegotiation authority.

To the Quality Review Board sitting as an administrative court of appeal, filed within fourteen calendar days of the penalty announcement.
To the Appellate Authority established under Section 36 of the Act, filed within ninety (90) days from the date of communication of the order.
To the local municipal district civil court in Mumbai, filed within twelve months accompanied by an appeal deposit of Rs. 10 Lakhs.
explanationCorrect: Section 36 provides that any member aggrieved by an order of the Board or Committee may appeal to the Appellate Authority within 90 days of communication.
explanationIncorrect: Appeals lie to the Appellate Authority under Section 36 within 90 days, not to the QRB, the Institute President, or a municipal district court.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 28 & Disciplinary Rules 2008, Rule 9
question: Under Section 28 of the Actuaries Act, 2006 and Rule 9 of the Disciplinary Rules 2008, what is the role of the Director (Discipline) and within what timeframe must a prima facie opinion be formed?
options: Conducts judicial trials, delivers final sentencing verdicts against respondents, and collects monetary disciplinary fines within 14 calendar days.
Audits the commercial books of the Institute and decides whether to approve annual membership certificate renewals for practicing consultants.
Serves as legal defense counsel for accused members before the Appellate Authority and cross-examines complainants during high court appeals.
Acts as the investigative gatekeeper, receives complaints/information, conducts preliminary examination, and issues a prima facie opinion within 60 days.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 28 and Rule 9, the Director (Discipline) investigates complaints/information and submits a prima facie opinion to the Board or Committee within 60 days.
explanationIncorrect: The Director (Discipline) is an investigative officer who forms a prima facie opinion; final adjudication is conducted by the Board of Discipline or Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 29 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what is the jurisdiction of the Board of Discipline and what maximum penalties can it impose?
options: Deals exclusively with First Schedule misconduct; can reprimand the member, suspend membership up to three months, or impose a fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh.
Deals with fee disputes between consulting actuaries and can order commercial compensation payments up to Rs. 25 Lakhs to the client.
Deals exclusively with Second Schedule misconduct; can permanently expel the member from the Institute or impose a fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
Deals with criminal fraud charges and can order custodial imprisonment for up to two years in a central correctional penitentiary.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 29, the Board of Discipline handles First Schedule matters and can reprimand, suspend membership up to 3 months, or fine up to Rs. 1 Lakh.
explanationIncorrect: First Schedule matters fall under the Board of Discipline (cap Rs. 1 Lakh, suspension up to 3 months). Second Schedule falls under the Disciplinary Committee.

question: Under Section 29B of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what is the jurisdiction of the Disciplinary Committee and what maximum penalties can it impose?
options: Deals exclusively with overseas actuarial bodies and can negotiate reciprocal exemption treaties with foreign professional councils.
Deals with Second Schedule or combined First and Second Schedule misconduct; can reprimand, remove permanently, or fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
Deals with internal staff grievances within the Secretariat and can adjust employee salaries or reassign departmental office workstations.
Deals exclusively with routine administrative fee defaults; can issue informal advisory warnings with zero authority to suspend practice licenses.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 29B, the Disciplinary Committee handles Second Schedule or combined cases and can reprimand, remove permanently/temporarily, or fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.
explanationIncorrect: The Disciplinary Committee handles grave misconduct under the Second Schedule, with powers to permanently expel members and fine up to Rs. 5 Lakhs.

question: Under Rules 4 and 5 of the Actuaries (Procedure for Enquiry of Professional and Other Misconduct) Rules, 2008, what are the statutory timelines for submitting the Written Statement and Rejoinder?
options: The respondent has 60 days to file a defense statement; the complainant has 90 days to lodge an interlocutory rejoinder petition before the Council.
There are zero statutory timelines; parties may submit pleadings at their leisure until the Council President formally schedules an oral hearing session.
The respondent has 21 days from receipt of complaint to submit a Written Statement; the complainant has 21 days from receipt of the statement to submit a Rejoinder.
The respondent has 10 calendar days to respond verbally; the complainant has 48 hours to file a formal cross-examination questionnaire before Council.
explanationCorrect: The Disciplinary Rules 2008 establish a symmetrical 21-day timeline: 21 days for the respondent's Written Statement, and 21 days for the complainant's Rejoinder.
explanationIncorrect: Pleadings follow strict statutory windows: exactly 21 days for Written Statement and 21 days for Rejoinder under Rules 4 and 5.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 31 (Powers of Civil Court)
question: Under Section 31 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, what legal powers are vested in the Disciplinary Directorate, the Board of Discipline, and the Disciplinary Committee?
options: Vested with full jurisdiction of a Criminal Sessions Court under the CrPC to conduct criminal trials and execute custodial sentences.
Vested with zero legal discovery powers; they can only review documents voluntarily provided by the complainant and accused member.
Vested with summary arbitral powers to modify commercial consulting fees and renegotiate contractual indemnities between corporate disputants.
Vested with the same powers as a Civil Court under CPC 1908: summoning witnesses, discovery/production of documents, and receiving evidence on affidavits.
explanationCorrect: Section 31 vests the disciplinary authorities with powers of a Civil Court under the CPC 1908: summoning persons, inspecting documents, and taking evidence on oath.
explanationIncorrect: Disciplinary tribunals exercise Civil Court powers under Section 31, not criminal sentencing powers or commercial contract renegotiation authority.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 6 (Prohibition on Soliciting Clients)
question: Actuary Kavita Nair, in public practice, sends unsolicited circular emails to Chief Financial Officers of all listed companies offering discounted pension valuation fees. Under the First Schedule, how is this conduct classified?
options: Professional misconduct in practice; an actuary in practice cannot solicit clients or professional work directly or indirectly by circulars, advertisements, or personal canvassing.
Legitimate commercial outreach; modern digital marketing principles permit direct email solicitation provided the technical fee schedule is disclosed.
A minor procedural irregularity that can be excused provided the actuary secures at least two corporate client appointments from the campaign.
Permissible conduct provided the solicitation emails are reviewed and approved in advance by the Institute's External Affairs Committee.
explanationCorrect: Clause 6 of Part I of the First Schedule explicitly classifies soliciting clients or professional work by circular, advertisement, or canvassing as professional misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Direct commercial solicitation of clients violates First Schedule Part I Clause 6, compromising professional dignity and public trust.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 8 (Duty to Communicate with Predecessor)
question: Actuary Suresh Iyer accepts an appointment as Appointed Actuary of an insurance company without first communicating in writing with the retiring actuary. Under the First Schedule, how is this characterized?
options: A commercial matter between the two actuaries that does not fall within the statutory disciplinary jurisdiction of the Institute of Actuaries of India.
Professional misconduct; accepting a position as an actuary previously held by another actuary without first communicating with them in writing constitutes statutory misconduct.
Misconduct only if the outgoing actuary had been dismissed by the corporate board of directors for reasons involving documented fraud.
Acceptable professional practice provided the new actuary completes the statutory valuation on time and files the required regulatory solvency forms.
explanationCorrect: Clause 8 of Part I of the First Schedule makes it professional misconduct to accept an appointment without first communicating in writing with the incumbent actuary.
explanationIncorrect: Written communication with the predecessor is a mandatory statutory duty under First Schedule Part I Clause 8; failure to do so constitutes misconduct.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 7 (Gross Negligence)
question: Actuary Meenakshi Sundaram signs a statutory valuation report certifying insurer solvency without reviewing policy data or testing claims triangles, resulting in massive insolvency. Under which Schedule does this gross negligence fall?
options: First Schedule Part II; gross negligence applies exclusively to salaried employees in commercial retail banks rather than consulting actuaries.
First Schedule Part I; routine mathematical calculation errors are minor professional infractions handled informally by the Board of Discipline.
Second Schedule Part I (Clause 7); gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties is a severe offence adjudicated by the Disciplinary Committee.
Exempt from disciplinary proceedings under the Actuaries Act provided the insurer's external auditors also signed off on the statutory accounts.
explanationCorrect: Gross negligence in the conduct of professional duties constitutes severe misconduct under Clause 7 of Part I of the Second Schedule, subject to permanent removal.
explanationIncorrect: Gross negligence falls under the Second Schedule (not First Schedule), carrying serious penalties up to permanent expulsion and Rs. 5 Lakhs fine.

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 5 & 6 (Concealing Material Misstatement)
question: An actuary knows that a client's financial statements contain a catastrophic 40% understatement of unearned premium reserves, but certifies the balance sheet without qualification. Under the Second Schedule, what is the consequence?
options: Subject to a mandatory maximum fine of Rs. 1,000 imposed by a local judicial magistrate with zero professional disciplinary consequences.
Immune from liability under Institute regulations because an actuary owes an absolute commercial fiduciary duty to protect client financial solvency.
Guilty only of a minor clerical omission that can be resolved by filing an amended addendum with the insurance company board within six months.
Guilty of professional misconduct under Second Schedule Part I for failing to report a material misstatement known to them or gross negligence.
explanationCorrect: Under Second Schedule Part I (Clauses 5 & 6), failing to disclose a material fact known to them or failing to report a material misstatement constitutes grave misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Concealing material reserve understatements constitutes severe Second Schedule misconduct, exposing the member to permanent expulsion by the Disciplinary Committee.

To the local municipal district civil court in Mumbai, filed within twelve months accompanied by an appeal deposit of Rs. 10 Lakhs.

To the President of the Institute of Actuaries of India sitting in executive chambers, filed within thirty calendar days of the decision.

explanationIncorrect: Appeals lie to the Appellate Authority under Section 36 within 90 days, not to the QRB, the Institute President, or a municipal district court.

question: Under Rules 4 and 5 of the Actuaries (Procedure for Enquiry of Professional and Other Misconduct) Rules, 2008, what are the statutory timelines for submitting the Written Statement and Rejoinder?

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Section 31 (Powers of Civil Court)

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 6 (Prohibition on Soliciting Clients)
question: Actuary Suresh Iyer, in public practice, sends unsolicited circular emails to Chief Financial Officers of all listed companies offering discounted pension valuation fees. Under the First Schedule, how is this conduct classified?

source: Actuaries Act 2006, First Schedule, Part I, Clause 8 (Duty to Communicate with Predecessor)
question: Actuary Meenakshi Sundaram accepts an appointment as Appointed Actuary of an insurance company without first communicating in writing with the retiring actuary. Under the First Schedule, how is this characterized?

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 7 (Gross Negligence)

source: Actuaries Act 2006, Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 5 & 6 (Concealing Material Misstatement)
question: An actuary knows that a client's financial statements contain a catastrophic 40% understatement of unearned premium reserves, but certifies the balance sheet without qualification. Under the Second Schedule, what is the consequence?

question: Under Section 36 of the Actuaries Act, 2006, where can a member aggrieved by an order of the Board of Discipline or Disciplinary Committee file an appeal, and within what timeframe?

Severe examination misconduct; subject to immediate exam cancellation, disciplinary inquiry, and potential multi-year or permanent debarment from IAI exams.

A laudable collaborative educational effort to assist less privileged actuarial candidates with post-examination syllabus revision and peer review.
A copyright infraction that can only be prosecuted if the Institute Council files a formal civil lawsuit in a commercial intellectual property court.

question: Student Aditya Joshi, who has passed seven Core Principles examinations, creates a LinkedIn profile describing themselves as a 'Consulting Actuary (FIAI)' and offers independent valuation services. Is this permissible?

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 2.2 (Professional Courtesy & Respect)
question: Disappointed by an exam result, Student Neha Gupta sends repeated threatening and abusive emails to Secretariat staff and examiners, accusing them of corruption without evidence. How is this behavior governed?

Legitimate consumer feedback protected under free speech rights that cannot be regulated or penalized by professional regulatory bodies.
Professional misconduct under the Student Code; members must maintain courtesy and respect, and refrain from abusive, defamatory, or threatening communications.
Permissible advocacy provided the student submits a formal re-evaluation fee within thirty calendar days of the abusive email transmission.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 3.3 (Plagiarism & Authentic Work)
question: Student Karthik Raman submits a mandatory predictive analytics model assignment by copying code and text verbatim from another candidate's project. How does the Student Code treat plagiarism?

Treated as an administrative deficiency requiring the student to re-submit the identical assignment within seven days without penalty.
Permissible technical collaboration provided both candidates share equal credit on the title slide of the final presentation deck.
Treated as serious academic dishonesty and misconduct; the assignment is disqualified and the candidate is referred for formal disciplinary action.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.3 treats plagiarism and copying assignments as serious misconduct, resulting in disqualification and referral to the Disciplinary Directorate.
explanationIncorrect: Plagiarism violates core ethical requirements of honesty and authentic work, carrying severe academic and disciplinary penalties.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 5 (Disciplinary Procedures for Students)
question: When a student member is formally accused of cheating in an IAI examination or committing other ethical misconduct, under what statutory framework is the matter investigated?
options: Referred to the Director (Discipline) and investigated under the Disciplinary Rules 2008 in the same statutory manner as qualified members.
Investigated exclusively by the Ministry of Education under national university campus student code of conduct guidelines.
Adjudicated informally by the examination supervisor in the examination hall with zero formal right of defense or evidence review.
Referred to a local student union council which votes on whether to forgive the candidate through an informal peer mediation process.
explanationCorrect: Section 5 of the Student Code provides that alleged misconduct is referred to the Director (Discipline) under the Actuaries Act and Disciplinary Rules 2008.
explanationIncorrect: Student misconduct is formally investigated under statutory quasi-judicial procedures by the Disciplinary Directorate under the 2008 Rules.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 4.2 (Prohibition on Signing Actuarial Reports)
question: An actuarial student working at an insurance consultancy is asked by management to sign an official gratuity valuation certificate as the 'Certifying Actuary'. What does the Student Code mandate?
options: The student may sign statutory reports if they have completed the Core Application and Specialist Principles examinations.
The student must refuse to sign; only Fellow members holding a valid Certificate of Practice are legally empowered to certify statutory reports.
The student may sign the report provided they add the word 'Student' in brackets beneath their handwritten signature.
The student can sign the report if the client board of directors approves the valuation results in an official board resolution.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 4.2 of the Student Code, students cannot sign statutory actuarial certificates or hold themselves out as authorized signing actuaries.
explanationIncorrect: Signing statutory reports is strictly restricted to qualified Fellow members holding a COP; students signing certificates commit statutory misconduct.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 3.1 (Impersonation Offence)
question: A candidate pays a senior actuarial professional to sit an online specialist examination on their behalf using forged credentials. What are the disciplinary consequences under the Student Code?
options: A monetary penalty of Rs. 5,000 payable to the Institute, with permission to re-sit the same examination at the subsequent examination diet.
A mandatory six-month suspension from booking examination sessions, with all prior exam credits remaining valid and intact on the student register.
Permanent expulsion of the student from membership, invalidation of all prior exam passes, and disciplinary action against the impersonator.
The candidate is required to sit a viva voce interview before the Education Committee to demonstrate equivalent technical proficiency.
explanationCorrect: Impersonation is the gravest examination offence, resulting in permanent expulsion, cancellation of passes, and referral of both parties for disciplinary prosecution.
explanationIncorrect: Impersonation destroys the integrity of qualifications and triggers permanent expulsion and criminal/statutory consequences, not minor fines.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 2.1 (Integrity in Professional Work)
question: An actuarial student discovers an error in a spreadsheet model that underestimates policyholder claims by 20%, but is told by their non-actuarial manager to keep quiet. What must the student do?
options: Comply with the manager's instruction, because student members are subordinates who owe absolute obedience to corporate line managers.
Resign immediately from the company without documenting the error, thereby discharging all professional and ethical responsibilities.
Delete the spreadsheet model completely from corporate servers so that neither management nor auditors can discover the error.
Uphold professional integrity and escalate the error through appropriate organizational or actuarial reporting channels to ensure correction.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 2.1, students must act with integrity and honesty, ensuring errors are escalated rather than concealed under commercial pressure.
explanationIncorrect: Subordinate status does not excuse concealing known material errors; students must maintain integrity and escalate through proper channels.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 1.2 (Binding Nature on All Students)
question: A registered student claims they were unaware of the Student Code of Conduct and therefore cannot be penalized for an examination infraction. How does the Code address ignorance of rules?
options: Ignorance of the Student Code is not a valid defense; all students agree to be bound by the Code and Institute regulations upon registration.
Ignorance is an absolute defense on the first occurrence of an infraction, requiring the Institute to issue an educational warning instead.
The Code is advisory only, leaving penalties to the sole discretion of the candidate's corporate employer.
The Code applies only to students who have physically attended an in-person professionalism induction orientation course in Mumbai.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 1.2, registration as a student implies full agreement to be bound by the Code. Ignorance of the Code is no defense.
explanationIncorrect: Ignorance of professional standards cannot be pleaded as a defense or mitigating factor in disciplinary inquiries.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 3.1 (Examination Integrity)
question: During an online proctored IAI examination, Student Sneha Pillai uses a secondary smartphone hidden off-camera to search for formulas and communicate with peers. Under the Student Code of Conduct, what is the consequence?
options: Permissible reference technique provided the candidate does not paste entire text paragraphs verbatim into the official answer submission box.
Severe examination misconduct; subject to immediate exam cancellation, disciplinary inquiry, and potential multi-year or permanent debarment from IAI exams.
Exempt from disciplinary proceedings provided the candidate registers for the same examination paper in the subsequent examination diet.
A minor procedural irregularity that results in a five-mark administrative deduction applied to the final calculated examination score.
explanationCorrect: Under the Student Code of Conduct Section 3.1, cheating, using unauthorized devices, or communicating during exams constitutes severe misconduct subject to cancellation and debarment.
explanationIncorrect: Cheating or using hidden phones during exams is an egregious ethical breach; it is not excused by mark deductions or subsequent re-registration.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 3.2 (Confidentiality of Exam Materials)
question: Student Aditya Joshi takes screenshots of live examination questions during a computer-based examination and posts them into a private Telegram study group. How is this conduct evaluated?
options: A copyright infraction that can only be prosecuted if the Institute Council files a formal civil lawsuit in a commercial intellectual property court.
Permissible conduct provided the candidate removes the screenshots within twenty-four hours after the official close of the examination window.
Severe breach of examination confidentiality and professional conduct, leading to immediate disciplinary investigation and potential expulsion from student membership.
A laudable collaborative educational effort to assist less privileged actuarial candidates with post-examination syllabus revision and peer review.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 3.2 of the Student Code, copying, photographing, or circulating live exam content constitutes grave misconduct subject to disciplinary expulsion.
explanationIncorrect: Distributing live exam materials compromises exam security, breaches student ethical duties, and triggers severe disciplinary sanctions under Section 3.2.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 4.1 (Prohibition on Holding Out)
question: Student Neha Gupta, who has passed seven Core Principles examinations, creates a LinkedIn profile describing themselves as a 'Consulting Actuary (FIAI)' and offers independent valuation services. Is this permissible?
options: Yes; the designation is permissible provided the candidate adds a profile disclaimer stating that Fellowship status is subject to final completion.
Yes; passing more than half of the actuarial examination curriculum legally entitles candidates to market themselves as provisional consulting actuaries.
No; students may describe themselves as Fellows in online profiles, but cannot use the abbreviation on physical printed business cards.
No; students are strictly prohibited from holding themselves out as qualified actuaries, using misleading credentials, or offering independent statutory services.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 4.1 of the Student Code, student members must never misrepresent their qualification level or hold themselves out as fully qualified actuaries.
explanationIncorrect: Misrepresenting student status as full Fellowship (FIAI) is a severe breach of integrity and illegal holding out under the Act and Student Code.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 2.2 (Professional Courtesy & Respect)
question: Disappointed by an exam result, Student Karthik Raman sends repeated threatening and abusive emails to Secretariat staff and examiners, accusing them of corruption without evidence. How is this behavior governed?
options: Professional misconduct under the Student Code; members must maintain courtesy and respect, and refrain from abusive, defamatory, or threatening communications.
An administrative disagreement that can only result in the candidate being temporarily blocked from accessing the Institute's online web portal.
Legitimate consumer feedback protected under free speech rights that cannot be regulated or penalized by professional regulatory bodies.
Permissible advocacy provided the student submits a formal re-evaluation fee within thirty calendar days of the abusive email transmission.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 2.2, students must maintain professional courtesy and respect. Abusive, defamatory, or threatening communications constitute misconduct.
explanationIncorrect: Abusing staff and examiners violates foundational professional standards of courtesy and respect, subjecting the student to formal disciplinary action.

source: Student Code of Conduct, Section 3.3 (Plagiarism & Authentic Work)
question: Student Pooja Chawla submits a mandatory predictive analytics model assignment by copying code and text verbatim from another candidate's project. How does the Student Code treat plagiarism?
options: Permissible technical collaboration provided both candidates share equal credit on the title slide of the final presentation deck.
Treated as serious academic dishonesty and misconduct; the assignment is disqualified and the candidate is referred for formal disciplinary action.
Treated as an administrative deficiency requiring the student to re-submit the identical assignment within seven days without penalty.
Acceptable practice because open-source programming conventions encourage sharing statistical algorithms across professional learning communities.
explanationCorrect: Section 3.3 treats plagiarism and copying assignments as serious misconduct, resulting in disqualification and referral to the Disciplinary Directorate.
explanationIncorrect: Plagiarism violates core ethical requirements of honesty and authentic work, carrying severe academic and disciplinary penalties.

Suspension or non-renewal of the Certificate of Practice, issuance of an official reprimand, and potential referral to the Disciplinary Directorate.
Automatic cancellation of Fellow membership and immediate forfeiture of all historical examination credentials and awards.
Zero professional consequences provided the actuary pays an additional late administrative fee of Rs. 200 alongside annual subscriptions.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 5.3, failure to comply with CPD can result in non-renewal/suspension of COP, administrative sanctions, and disciplinary action.
explanationIncorrect: Non-compliance directly threatens the member's Certificate of Practice (COP) and triggers disciplinary proceedings; it is not a trivial late-fee matter.

question: A Category 1 actuary completes 15 hours of technical actuarial CPD, 4 hours of professional conduct CPD, and 12 hours of general business leadership courses. What is the total verifiable CPD recognized under APS 9?
options: 31 hours; all verifiable hours in any business subject are recognized without limitation towards the 24-hour annual requirement.
24 hours; excess general business hours automatically convert to fulfill deficiencies in professional conduct and ethical requirements.
22 hours; because general/other verifiable hours are capped at a maximum of 3 hours, and the actuary is deficient by 2 hours in professional conduct.
15 hours; general business leadership courses are strictly excluded and cannot contribute towards actuarial CPD under any circumstances.
explanationCorrect: Under Category 1: min 15 tech, min 6 conduct, max 3 other. Here, other is capped at 3 (15 + 4 + 3 = 22 hrs). Furthermore, conduct is deficient by 2 hrs (4 vs 6 req).
explanationIncorrect: Other verifiable hours are capped at 3 hours. General hours cannot substitute for the mandatory 6 hours of professional conduct.

question: Which of the following topics satisfies the mandatory 'Professional Conduct & Ethics' CPD requirement under APS 9 Section 2.3?
options: Training on advanced neural network machine learning coding syntax in Python with zero coverage of professional ethical considerations.
Lectures on macroeconomic interest rate forecasting models and currency exchange rate arbitrage pricing in international financial markets.
Commercial sales negotiation tactics designed to increase consulting firm billings and cross-sell reinsurance advisory services to clients.
Sessions on PCS v4.0, actuarial professional standards, ethical dilemma analysis, disciplinary procedures, and statutory regulatory compliance.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 2.3, professional conduct CPD covers professional standards (PCS), ethics, disciplinary processes, governance, and relevant regulatory law.
explanationIncorrect: Pure mathematical modeling, macroeconomic forecasts, and commercial sales tactics do not qualify as professional conduct CPD.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 3.4 (Pro-rata Calculation for New COP Holders)
question: A Fellow member is granted a Certificate of Practice on 1 October, halfway through the financial year. How are their CPD requirements determined under APS 9 Section 3.4?
options: CPD requirements are applied on a pro-rata basis for the remaining portion of the year, rounded up to the nearest whole hour.
The member is completely exempt from all CPD obligations until the commencement of the subsequent full financial year on 1 April.
The member must complete the full 24 hours of Category 1 CPD within the remaining six months with zero pro-rata allowance permitted.
The member must complete double the hours in the subsequent year to compensate for the partial year of initial Certificate of Practice grant.
explanationCorrect: Under Section 3.4, members joining a category mid-year are assessed on a pro-rata basis for the balance of the compliance year.
explanationIncorrect: Mid-year entrants are subject to pro-rata requirements rounded to whole hours, not full-year burdens or blanket waivers.

source: APS 9 (v4.00), Section 3.1 (Category 1 COP Holder Mandatory Hours)
question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 3.1, what are the mandatory annual CPD requirements for Category 1 members (Fellows holding an active Certificate of Practice)?
options: CPD is voluntary for senior COP holders with over fifteen years of continuous practice experience, requiring only a signed self-certification waiver.
Minimum 24 verifiable CPD hours per year: at least 15 hours technical in primary practice, at least 6 hours professional/ethical, and max 3 hours other.
Minimum 40 CPD hours per year, all of which may be completed through unverified personal reading of business newspapers and actuarial textbooks.
Minimum 15 verifiable hours per year: at least 9 hours technical and 3 hours professional, with zero restriction on non-verifiable informal webinars.
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 Section 3.1, Category 1 COP holders must complete at least 24 verifiable hours annually: min 15 technical, min 6 professional, max 3 other.
explanationIncorrect: Category 1 requires 24 verifiable hours (15 technical, 6 professional/ethical, max 3 other). Unverified reading or waivers do not satisfy Category 1.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 3.2, what are the mandatory annual CPD requirements for Category 2 members (Fellows not holding a Certificate of Practice)?
options: Minimum 24 verifiable hours per year: at least 15 hours technical and 6 hours professional, identical to the requirement for active COP holders.
Exempt from all annual CPD requirements until the member formally applies to the Council for the grant of a Certificate of Practice.
Minimum 15 verifiable CPD hours per year: at least 9 hours technical in primary area, at least 3 hours professional/ethical, and max 3 hours other.
Minimum 10 verifiable hours per year, comprising exclusively non-technical leadership communication skills and corporate human resources personnel management training.
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 Section 3.2, Category 2 members must complete at least 15 verifiable hours annually: min 9 technical, min 3 professional, max 3 other.
explanationIncorrect: Category 2 requires 15 verifiable hours (9 technical, 3 professional, max 3 other). Category 1 requires 24 hours; Category 2 is not exempt.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 3.3, what are the mandatory annual CPD requirements for Category 3 members (Associate members of the Institute)?
options: Minimum 5 hours of non-verifiable informal technical discussion with an appointed Fellowship mentor documented in a personal unverified diary.
Minimum 24 verifiable CPD hours per year, requiring the exact same distribution and subject specialization as senior Appointed Actuaries.
Exempt from CPD obligations provided they are actively studying for fellowship examinations and have attempted at least one paper during the year.
Minimum 10 verifiable CPD hours per year: at least 6 hours technical in primary area, at least 2 hours professional/ethical, and max 2 hours other.
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 Section 3.3, Category 3 Associates must complete at least 10 verifiable hours: min 6 technical, min 2 professional, max 2 other.
explanationIncorrect: Associates must complete 10 verifiable CPD hours annually; studying for exams does not provide an automatic blanket exemption from APS 9.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 2.1, which of the following activities satisfies the criteria to be counted as 'Verifiable CPD'?
options: Attending structured seminars, conferences, or webinars with formal attendance logs, presenting technical papers, or serving on working groups.
Informal personal browsing of financial websites and reading unverified social media commentary during evening leisure hours at home.
Performing routine salaried valuation calculations in the actuary's regular employment that are repeated monthly as core job deliverables.
Discussing internal corporate politics or negotiating commercial consulting fees during an informal social luncheon with prospective clients.
explanationCorrect: Verifiable CPD requires structured learning with independent verification: seminars with logs, paper presentations, serving on technical groups, etc.
explanationIncorrect: Routine day-to-day employment tasks, informal reading, and commercial social lunches do not qualify as verifiable CPD under APS 9.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 4.2, for what minimum period must a member retain all verifiable CPD evidence, certificates, and event logs?
options: Exactly one (1) year until the member's annual membership subscription renewal is processed and acknowledged by the Secretariat.
A minimum period of five (5) years from the end of the relevant CPD compliance year, available for inspection upon audit by Council.
Zero retention requirement; once the member submits the annual declaration online, all underlying certificates may be immediately discarded.
A minimum period of ten (10) years in accordance with the statutory document retention rules of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 Section 4.2, members must maintain verifiable CPD records for at least 5 years from the end of the relevant compliance year.
explanationIncorrect: The mandatory retention period for CPD evidence under APS 9 is 5 years (unlike audit workpapers under FT-IGN 31 which require 7 years).

question: How does the Council of the Institute monitor and enforce compliance with APS 9 Continuing Professional Development obligations under Section 5.1?
options: Council relies exclusively on an honor system with zero audits, investigations, or documentary verification procedures at any time.
Council requires all members to physically present their original paper seminar tickets at the Institute head office in Navi Mumbai in person.
Council conducts random and risk-based audits of member CPD records annually, requiring selected members to submit supporting documentary proof.
Council sends inspectors to observe every practicing actuary at their physical commercial office desks for one full week every calendar year.
explanationCorrect: Section 5.1 provides that Council conducts periodic random and risk-based audits, requiring selected members to submit evidence of claimed CPD hours.
explanationIncorrect: CPD compliance is enforced through systematic random and targeted audits where members must produce verifiable proof within specified timelines.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 3.3, what are the mandatory annual CPD requirements for Category 3 members (Associate members of the Institute)?
options: Minimum 24 verifiable CPD hours per year, requiring the exact same distribution and subject specialization as senior Appointed Actuaries.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 2.1, which of the following activities satisfies the criteria to be counted as 'Verifiable CPD'?
options: Discussing internal corporate politics or negotiating commercial consulting fees during an informal social luncheon with prospective clients.
Informal personal browsing of financial websites and reading unverified social media commentary during evening leisure hours at home.
Attending structured seminars, conferences, or webinars with formal attendance logs, presenting technical papers, or serving on working groups.
Performing routine salaried valuation calculations in the actuary's regular employment that are repeated monthly as core job deliverables.
explanationCorrect: Verifiable CPD requires structured learning with independent verification: seminars with logs, paper presentations, serving on technical groups, etc.
explanationIncorrect: Routine day-to-day employment tasks, informal reading, and commercial social lunches do not qualify as verifiable CPD under APS 9.

question: Under APS 9 (v4.00) Section 4.2, for what minimum period must a member retain all verifiable CPD evidence, certificates, and event logs?
options: Zero retention requirement; once the member submits the annual declaration online, all underlying certificates may be immediately discarded.
A minimum period of ten (10) years in accordance with the statutory document retention rules of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.
Exactly one (1) year until the member's annual membership subscription renewal is processed and acknowledged by the Secretariat.
A minimum period of five (5) years from the end of the relevant CPD compliance year, available for inspection upon audit by Council.
explanationCorrect: Under APS 9 Section 4.2, members must maintain verifiable CPD records for at least 5 years from the end of the relevant compliance year.
explanationIncorrect: The mandatory retention period for CPD evidence under APS 9 is 5 years (unlike audit workpapers under FT-IGN 31 which require 7 years).

question: How does the Council of the Institute monitor and enforce compliance with APS 9 Continuing Professional Development obligations under Section 5.1?

explanationCorrect: Section 5.1 provides that Council conducts periodic random and risk-based audits, requiring selected members to submit evidence of claimed CPD hours.

question: Actuary Sunita Deshmukh, an active COP holder, fails to complete mandatory CPD hours and cannot produce verifiable proof upon audit. What consequences follow under APS 9?

question: Which of the following topics satisfies the mandatory 'Professional Conduct & Ethics' CPD requirement under APS 9 Section 2.3?
